scenes.narration: Picture one giant open-plan office. Every announcement reaches every desk. That's a flat network. Let's split it into floors, using something called a V L A N.

scenes.heading: The apartment building
scenes.narration: Think of an apartment building with one hundred flats. Each floor is its own V L A N. Mail only gets delivered to flats on the same floor. The sticker on each letter says which floor it belongs to. A flat's front door only belongs to one floor, and that's an access port. The shared stairwell that carries every floor is called a trunk.

scenes.heading: Setting one up
scenes.narration: Setting one up takes three steps. First, create the V L A N on the switch. Second, put the port in access mode. Third, assign that port to the V L A N. Then check your work.

steps.title: Create the VLAN
steps.sub: vlan 10 and give it a name

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three mix-ups catch people out. A V L A N is a Layer two idea, not Layer three. A trunk port carries lots of floors at once, not just one. And the native V L A N doesn't have to be number one. Pick an unused one for safety.

items.wrong: A VLAN is a Layer 3 concept
items.right: It's Layer 2; subnets just map onto it

items.wrong: A trunk carries only one VLAN

items.right: Any VLAN works; use an unused one

scenes.heading: Remember this
scenes.narration: So, to recap. A V L A N splits one switch into separate floors. Access ports belong to one floor, and trunks carry many. And create the V L A N before you assign ports to it. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva VLAN lab.

points.t: A VLAN splits one switch into separate floors
Access ports: one VLAN. Trunks: many
Create the VLAN before assigning ports
